title: Reconciliation: can I come back?
hookLine: the fear of mortal sin keeps people away for years; the sacrament of return is a door, not a wall

lines: A STRAIGHT ANSWER, AND A KIND ONE.
cards: A text at one in the morning, typed and deleted three times, to the one friend who still goes to Mass. Is it true I can't come back until I confess? I haven't been in six years.
Am I in mortal sin? Do I have to fix everything first? The friend isn't sure either.
So the question goes back in the drawer for another year. Plenty of people carry some version of that text. It deserves a straight answer, and a kind one.

teach.h: WHAT MAKES A SIN MORTAL: ALL THREE.
teach.b: First, what the Church teaches, unsoftened. The Catechism says skipping Sunday Mass on purpose, with no serious reason, is a grave matter.

Being sick, caring for someone, or being somewhere with no Mass within reach is not a sin at all. For a sin to be mortal, three things must all be true at once: grave matter, full knowledge, and deliberate consent.

More on that later in the year. Then the Catechism adds: we can judge that an act is wrong, but the judgment of persons belongs to God alone. Nobody gets to pronounce a verdict on your soul from the parking lot.
Not even you. Second, what to do.

teach.h: MASS IS OPEN. CONFESSION IS THE DOOR.
teach.b: Mass is open; you can go this Sunday. If there may be serious sin, Catholics wait on Communion and go to confession first. That isn't a fee at the door.
It is the door. The name says so: reconciliation, from the Latin reconciliare, to bring together again. Jesus tells of a son who wastes everything and walks home with a speech rehearsed.

In the Douay-Rheims: "when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and running to him fell upon his neck, and kissed him." The father runs before the speech is done.

teach.h: SCRUPULOSITY: WHEN FEAR WON'T LET GO.
teach.b: Third, when the fear won't let go. Some confess, hear the words of forgiveness, and still can't believe it. They check and recheck every thought for sin.
Catholic spiritual writers have an old name for this: scrupulosity. The Church meets it gently. A steady confessor helps, and so can a good counselor; it isn't a lack of faith.
Fourth, the feeling afterward. Some walk out in tears of relief. Some feel awkward, or nothing at all.
Catholics believe the forgiveness is just as real either way.

how: Catholics who have been away can return to Mass at any time; those aware of serious sin go to confession before receiving Communion. Many parishes offer confession on Saturday afternoons, and priests are used to hearing 'it's been a long time, and I don't remember how.'

o: a public apology made in front of the parish
a penalty you pay before you may return to Mass
the sacrament of confession, of coming back to God

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: fear that won't believe it's forgiven
runs before the speech is done

s: you have to go to confession before you're allowed back into Mass
Mass is open to anyone. confession comes before receiving Communion, if there may be serious sin.
missing Mass because you were sick is a sin
a serious reason, like illness or caring for someone, excuses it.
Catholics believe forgiveness in confession is real even if you feel nothing
the sacrament doesn't depend on the feeling afterward.

games.q: you're the father. your son who left and spent everything is walking up the road, a great way off, rehearsing a speech. what do you do?
o: wait on the porch for his apology.
run to him, embrace him and kiss him.
send a servant to ask what he wants.
games.why: he runs. "moved with compassion, and running to him fell upon his neck, and kissed him." the speech hardly gets started.

practice: Picture yourself on a long road home, going over what you'd say. Far off, someone has already seen you and is running; don't finish the speech, let yourself be met halfway, with whatever you carry, as it is.
If you pray, hand it to God in a word.

wordCard.voice: Reconciliation. The sacrament of return, where Catholics confess to a priest and hear that they're forgiven: a door, not a wall. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: to bring together again, to restore; from re- and conciliare, to bring together.

carryVoice: Your line: there's always a way back. No one is too far away. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and running to him fell upon his neck, and kissed him.
